units.title: Power and authority in the modern world, 1919 to 1946

points.title: The postwar settlement
points.brief: The peace treaties redrew Europe's borders and left many people, especially in Germany, Italy and Hungary, resentful of the terms.

points.title: The League of Nations
points.brief: Set up to keep peace through collective security, the League lacked an army and the United States never joined, so it failed to stop aggression in the 1930s.

points.title: Challenges to democracy
points.brief: New democracies faced economic crisis, political violence and distrust, and many gave way to authoritarian rule between the wars.

points.title: The Great Depression
points.brief: After the 1929 Wall Street crash, world trade collapsed and unemployment soared, which drove voters towards extreme parties.

points.title: Fascism in Italy
points.brief: Mussolini's Fascists used violence and the March on Rome in 1922 to take power, then built a one-party state.

points.title: The Nazi rise to power
points.brief: Hitler's Nazi Party grew during the Depression, he became chancellor in January 1933, and the Enabling Act let him rule as a dictator.

points.title: Militarism in Japan
points.brief: In the 1930s the army gained control of Japan's government and pursued expansion, invading Manchuria in 1931 and China in 1937.

points.title: Stalin's Soviet Union
points.brief: Stalin built a dictatorship through a cult of personality, forced industrialisation and terror against real and imagined enemies.

points.title: Methods of control
points.brief: Dictatorships used propaganda, secret police, censorship, youth movements and terror to hold power and win or force support.

chapters.title: The road to World War II

points.title: Aggression in the 1930s
points.brief: Japan's invasion of Manchuria, Italy's invasion of Ethiopia and Germany's rearmament and takeover of the Rhineland, Austria and Czechoslovakia went largely unchecked.

points.title: Appeasement
points.brief: Britain and France gave in to some of Hitler's demands, as at Munich in 1938, hoping to avoid war. Historians still debate whether it was a mistake.

points.title: The outbreak of war in 1939
points.brief: The Nazi-Soviet Pact cleared the way for Germany to invade Poland on 1 September 1939, and Britain and France declared war.

points.title: The Holocaust
points.brief: Nazi Germany murdered about six million Jews, as well as Roma, disabled people and others, in a planned genocide.

points.title: The world after 1945
points.brief: The war ended with the defeat of Germany and Japan, the founding of the United Nations, and the United States and Soviet Union as rival superpowers.

units.title: Russia and the Soviet Union, 1917 to 1941

points.title: The February Revolution of 1917
points.brief: War losses, food shortages and strikes led the Tsar to abdicate. A Provisional Government shared power with the Petrograd Soviet.

points.title: The October Revolution
points.brief: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd in October 1917, promising peace, land and bread.

points.title: Civil war and War Communism
points.brief: The Bolsheviks' Red Army defeated the Whites by 1921. War Communism took grain and industry under state control and caused famine.

points.title: The New Economic Policy
points.brief: In 1921 Lenin allowed small private trade and farming to restore the economy, which divided the Communist Party.

points.title: Stalin's rise to power
points.brief: After Lenin died in 1924, Stalin used his post as general secretary to build support and defeat rivals such as Trotsky.

points.title: Collectivisation
points.brief: From 1929 peasants were forced onto collective farms. Resistance, seizures of grain and famine killed millions, especially in Ukraine.

points.title: The Five-Year Plans
points.brief: Plans from 1928 set huge targets for heavy industry, building new factories and cities at great human cost.

points.title: The Great Terror
points.brief: In the purges of 1936 to 1938, hundreds of thousands were executed and many more sent to Gulag labour camps, including party leaders and army officers.

points.title: Society and culture under Stalin
points.brief: Art, education and religion were controlled to serve the state, and women were expected to work and raise families.

points.title: The end of French rule
points.brief: The Viet Minh defeated France at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. The Geneva Accords split Vietnam in two until elections that were never held.

points.title: The two Vietnams
points.brief: The communist North under Ho Chi Minh faced the US-backed South, where the Viet Cong fought the government.

points.title: United States involvement
points.brief: Fearing communism would spread, the United States sent advisers and, after the Gulf of Tonkin incident in 1964, combat troops. Australia also sent troops.

points.title: The nature of the war
points.brief: The Viet Cong and North Vietnamese used guerrilla tactics, while the United States relied on bombing and search and destroy missions.

points.title: The Tet Offensive
points.brief: The 1968 attacks across South Vietnam were a military defeat for the communists but turned many Americans against the war.

points.title: Opposition to the war
points.brief: Protests grew in the United States and Australia, including the Moratorium marches of 1970, fed by conscription and casualties.

points.title: Withdrawal and the fall of Saigon
points.brief: US troops left after the 1973 Paris Peace Accords, and North Vietnam took Saigon in April 1975.

points.title: Cambodia and the Khmer Rouge
points.brief: The Khmer Rouge took power in 1975 and caused the deaths of about 1.5 to 2 million Cambodians before Vietnam invaded in 1979.

points.title: Effects of the conflict
points.brief: Millions died, the land was damaged by bombing and chemicals, and many refugees fled by boat, some resettling in Australia.

points.title: Origins of the Cold War
points.brief: Distrust between the United States and the Soviet Union grew after 1945 as Europe divided into Western and Soviet blocs.

points.title: A bipolar world
points.brief: The superpowers led rival alliances, NATO and the Warsaw Pact, competed for influence and avoided fighting each other directly.

points.title: The nuclear arms race
points.brief: Both sides built huge nuclear arsenals. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought them close to war and led to efforts to control arms.

points.title: The end of the Cold War
points.brief: Gorbachev's reforms, the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 ended the Cold War.

points.title: A single superpower
points.brief: After 1991 the United States was the only superpower, and the 1990s saw hopes for cooperation through the UN.

points.title: Conflicts after the Cold War
points.brief: Wars in the former Yugoslavia and genocide in Rwanda in the 1990s tested the UN and the will of other countries to step in.

points.title: Terrorism and the response
points.brief: The attacks of 11 September 2001 led to the US-led war in Afghanistan and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.

points.title: The rise of new powers
points.brief: The fast growth of China and other economies began to shift global power away from the United States by 2011.

points.title: The United Nations and world order
points.brief: The UN's peacekeeping and humanitarian work grew, but Security Council vetoes often blocked action.
